x.A: After 30 days the access pattern for each object is inconsistent. Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves each object between tiers based on its use, which saves cost with no retrieval fees and keeps multi-AZ resiliency.
x.B: Because the company uses multipart uploads, incomplete uploads can leave behind parts that keep costing money. A lifecycle rule that cleans them up removes that waste.
x.C: Cleaning up expired delete markers applies to versioned buckets, and the company overwrites objects rather than using versioning.
x.D: Standard-IA charges retrieval fees, which add up when access is inconsistent, so it isn't the best choice.
x.E: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so it doesn't meet the high availability and resiliency requirement.

x.A: AWS Network Firewall with domain list rule groups filters outbound traffic by domain name. Routing the private subnet's outbound traffic through it allows only the approved repositories and blocks everything else.
x.B: AWS WAF filters inbound web requests to ALB, CloudFront, or API Gateway. It doesn't filter outbound traffic from EC2 instances.
x.C: Security groups work with IP addresses and ports, not URLs, so they can't allow only specific URLs.
x.D: An ALB handles inbound traffic and doesn't act as an outbound proxy for internet access.

x.A: Increasing the number of EC2 instances manually doesn't handle a sudden spike and isn't guaranteed to process all requests.
x.B: Auto Scaling on network traffic helps, but new instances take time to launch, and requests could be lost or time out during a sudden spike.
x.C: ElastiCache in front of the ALB isn't a valid design and caching doesn't help with sales requests that need processing.
x.D: CloudFront serves static content, and an SQS queue stores incoming sales requests durably so the EC2 workers process them as capacity allows. No request is lost during a surge.

x.A: Macie finds sensitive data in S3 and doesn't scan EC2 for software vulnerabilities, and cron jobs on each instance mean no central patching or reporting.
x.B: GuardDuty detects threats and doesn't scan for software vulnerabilities, and Session Manager is for shell access, not scheduled patching.
x.C: Detective investigates security findings and doesn't scan for vulnerabilities. An EventBridge rule doesn't patch instances by itself and doesn't report patch status.
x.D: Inspector scans EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities, and Systems Manager Patch Manager patches them on a schedule and reports each instance's patch compliance.

x.A: Creating a KMS key and enabling encryption on the DB instances encrypts the data at rest, including its storage, backups, and replicas.
x.B: Secrets Manager stores secrets such as passwords, not encryption keys used to encrypt RDS storage.
x.C: An ACM certificate enables SSL/TLS, which protects data in transit, not at rest.
x.D: An IAM certificate also covers TLS, which is encryption in transit and not at rest.

x.A: At 15 Mbps with a 70% cap, 20 TB would take years to upload, so a Snowball device that is shipped back to AWS is the way to finish within 30 days.
x.B: DataSync would still send data over the limited network link, which is far too slow for 20 TB.
x.C: A VPN uses the same limited bandwidth, so it can't move 20 TB in 30 days.
x.D: Transfer Acceleration helps with long-distance transfers but doesn't increase the available bandwidth at the data center.

x.A: A file server on EC2 in a public subnet exposes confidential files to the internet and still has capacity limits.
x.B: FSx for Windows File Server scales storage and integrates with the existing Active Directory so only authorized users get access. Client VPN lets remote employees connect securely and download files.
x.C: A signed URL gives anyone with the link access, which doesn't ensure only authorized users, and doesn't fit Windows file shares.
x.D: A public VPC endpoint isn't a thing, and S3 isn't a drop-in Windows file share.

x.A: CloudFront in front of the ALB caches content but doesn't help with CPU-intensive batch calculations on the servers.
x.B: A simple scaling policy based on CPU reacts only after CPU is already at 100%, so the slowdown happens first, and instances take time to launch.
x.C: Scheduled scaling adds capacity before midnight on the first of each month, so the instances are ready when the batch begins and the application isn't disrupted.
x.D: A cache doesn't take off the CPU load of the batch calculation.

x.A: Transfer Family provides a managed SFTP endpoint for S3 and can authenticate against Active Directory, so the customer's SFTP client works unchanged and no servers are needed.
x.B: DMS migrates databases and doesn't give SFTP access to S3 or authenticate by Active Directory.
x.C: DataSync synchronizes data and isn't an SFTP server for the customer's application, and IAM Identity Center isn't an SFTP login.
x.D: A Windows EC2 instance with SFTP is a server you have to manage, which adds operational overhead.

x.A: Registering an AMI from a snapshot and swapping it with Step Functions doesn't remove the lazy loading delay when instances launch.
x.B: EBS fast snapshot restore on the snapshot behind the AMI makes volumes fully initialized when instances launch, so large instances start with minimum initialization latency.
x.C: DLM automates creating AMIs and snapshots but doesn't speed up the initialization of volumes at launch.
x.D: AWS Backup lifecycle policies manage backups, not launch latency.

x.A: Secrets Manager encrypts the secret with a KMS key and has built-in rotation for Aurora, with a custom schedule of 14 days. It needs the least operational effort.
x.B: Parameter Store has no native rotation, so you would build a Lambda function to rotate the password.
x.C: Credentials in a file on EFS with a custom Lambda rotation means building and maintaining all the rotation logic.
x.D: A credentials file in S3 with a custom Lambda rotation is a lot of custom work, and the application has to keep re-downloading the file.

x.A: Aurora MySQL replicas read from the same shared storage volume, so replica lag is typically milliseconds, and Aurora Auto Scaling manages the replicas. Aurora native functions replace the stored procedures with minimal code changes.
x.B: A cache doesn't reduce the lag of the read replicas, and rewriting stored procedures as Lambda functions requires code changes.
x.C: Self-managed MySQL on EC2 increases operational overhead and doesn't reduce replication lag by much.
x.D: DynamoDB is a different data model and would need large code changes, so it isn't a minimal-change option.

x.A: Binary log replication to an Aurora cluster with a running instance has replication lag, needs management, and costs more.
x.B: An Aurora global database replicates storage to the secondary Region. After setup, you can remove the secondary DB instance and keep only the replicated storage, which is the cheapest. You can add an instance during a disaster.
x.C: DMS replication needs a replication instance and continuous management, and it adds cost.
x.D: Keeping at least one DB instance in the secondary Region costs more than keeping only the replicated storage.

x.A: KMS manages encryption keys, not database credentials, and it can't rotate a database user's password.
x.B: A custom Lambda rotation function needs to be written and maintained, but Secrets Manager has built-in rotation for RDS MySQL.
x.C: Secrets Manager stores the credentials, and its built-in rotation schedule rotates the database user's password with no custom code. Only a small change is needed to load credentials from Secrets Manager.
x.D: Parameter Store has no built-in credential rotation.

x.A: AWS WAF in front of the ALB with web ACLs that include SQL injection rules blocks those requests before they reach the application.
x.B: An ALB listener rule can only return a fixed response for matching conditions and doesn't inspect request content for SQL injection.
x.C: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS attacks, not SQL injection.
x.D: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and doesn't block attacks.

x.A: EMR to load into SPICE adds a cluster to manage, and it doesn't use Lake Formation's governance for column-level control.
x.B: IAM policies can't enforce column-level access to the data, and Glue Studio ingestion needs more setup.
x.C: S3 bucket policies can't enforce column-level access, and Glue Elastic Views has been retired.
x.D: A Lake Formation blueprint ingests data from the database into the data lake, Lake Formation enforces column-level permissions, and Athena is the data source for QuickSight. It requires the least work.

x.A: A dynamic scaling policy at 60% CPU reacts after the load begins, but the capacity is needed 30 minutes before the jobs run.
x.B: Scheduled scaling needs someone to determine the capacity numbers, and the company doesn't have the resources to analyze capacity trends.
x.C: Predictive scaling learns from the history and forecasts the load, pre-launching instances 30 minutes before the jobs run, with no manual capacity analysis.
x.D: Invoking Lambda when CPU reaches 60% is reactive, custom, and needs code to maintain.

x.A: Self-managing MySQL replication on EC2 across Regions is a lot of operational work.
x.B: RDS Multi-AZ and read replicas across AZs stay within one Region, so they don't provide a multi-Region DR design.
x.C: An Aurora global database replicates data to another Region automatically with typically about a second of lag, with the least operational work for multi-Region DR.
x.D: Restoring from backups copied to S3 CRR takes longer and requires manual steps, which means more operational work and a slower recovery.

x.A: The SQS Extended Client Library for Java stores large messages (up to 2 GB) in S3 and sends a pointer in the SQS message, so the Java application needs only small code changes.
x.B: EventBridge events also have a size limit of 256 KB, and switching services would mean larger changes.
x.C: The SQS message size limit of 256 KB can't be raised to 50 MB.
x.D: Referencing messages stored in EFS would need custom code to write and read them, so it's more change.

x.A: Cognito provides low-cost, scalable authentication for a small user base, Lambda@Edge authorizes requests at CloudFront edge locations for low latency, and CloudFront serves the application globally. It's all serverless.
x.B: Directory Service for Microsoft AD costs much more for under 100 users, and an ALB doesn't serve content globally.
x.C: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads to S3 and doesn't serve a web application globally, and Lambda in one Region adds latency.
x.D: Directory Service costs more, and Elastic Beanstalk is not a global serverless serving layer.

x.A: A volume gateway presents block storage over iSCSI, so it doesn't provide SMB and NFS file shares or S3 objects.
x.B: A tape gateway is for virtual tape backups and doesn't present SMB and NFS shares.
x.C: FSx File Gateway gives access to FSx for Windows File Server, which isn't S3, and it doesn't support NFS shares.
x.D: An S3 File Gateway presents SMB and NFS file shares backed by S3 objects, with a local cache for frequently accessed data. S3 Lifecycle policies can then tier the inactive data.

x.A: A Compute Savings Plan gives savings across instance families and sizes, so the company can change them in the next 6 months and still keep the discount for 3 years.
x.B: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is tied to a specific instance family in a Region, so changing the family would lose the discount.
x.C: Zonal Reserved Instances are tied to a specific instance type and AZ, so they aren't flexible.
x.D: Standard Reserved Instances lock in an instance family, so they can't be changed freely.

x.A: Constant, predictable traffic suits provisioned mode with reserved capacity, which has the lowest price, and Standard-IA lowers storage cost for data accessed less often. This keeps spending within the budget.
x.B: Provisioned mode alone works but doesn't use reserved capacity or the lower-cost table class, so it costs more.
x.C: On-demand costs more per request for a constant workload, and you don't set RCUs and WCUs in on-demand mode.
x.D: On-demand mode doesn't use reserved capacity, and you don't specify RCUs and WCUs there.

x.A: Copying a snapshot to an unencrypted one would expose the confidential data and isn't allowed for encrypted Aurora snapshots.
x.B: A snapshot encrypted with a customer managed key can be shared if the other account is allowed to use the KMS key. Adding the acquiring account to the key policy and sharing the snapshot lets them restore it securely.
x.C: Snapshots encrypted with the AWS managed key can't be shared with another account, and a key alias doesn't give access.
x.D: Aurora snapshots can't be downloaded and uploaded to S3 like that, and it would expose the data.

x.A: Multi-AZ gives the high availability and automatic failover the company needs for the SQL Server instance.
x.B: Restoring a snapshot to a new deployment creates a separate copy that isn't kept in sync, so it doesn't help with high availability or ongoing reporting.
x.C: A read replica handles the reporting queries so transactions on the primary aren't slowed down.
x.D: RDS Custom gives OS access and doesn't improve availability or reporting performance.
x.E: RDS Proxy pools connections and doesn't limit reports to a maintenance window.
